propositions.text: Applicants challenge a Senior Immigration Officer's January 23, 2020 refusal of their second permanent residence application on humanitarian and compassionate grounds.
propositions.quote: The Applicants challenge a negative decision of a Senior Immigration Officer [Officer] dated January 23, 2020 refusing the Applicants’ second application for permanent residence based on humanitarian and compassionate [H&C] grounds under section 25 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA].

paragraphs.summary: The Applicants challenge a Senior Immigration Officer's January 23, 2020 refusal of their second permanent residence application on humanitarian and compassionate grounds.

propositions.text: Applicants are Brazilian spouses with a long immigration history including exclusion orders and unsuccessful applications.
propositions.quote: The Applicants are spouses and citizens of Brazil. They have a lengthy immigration history of entering and leaving Canada, facing exclusion orders, and submitting unsuccessful work permit, temporary resident visa, pre-removal risk assessment and H&C applications.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants are Brazilian spouses with a long immigration history including exclusion orders and unsuccessful applications.

propositions.text: Applicants submitted a second H&C application on September 12, 2018, citing establishment in Canada and adverse conditions in Brazil.
propositions.quote: On September 12, 2018, the Applicants submitted a second H&C application, requesting that the Officer consider their establishment in Canada and the adverse country conditions in Brazil.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants submitted a second H&C application on September 12, 2018, citing establishment in Canada and adverse conditions in Brazil.

propositions.text: Officer refused the second H&C application on January 23, 2020, considering Applicants' factors and best interests of a 16-year-old family friend who supported the application.
propositions.quote: On January 23, 2020, the Officer refused the Applicants’ second H&C application. The Officer considered the two factors raised by the Applicants, as well as the best interests of a 16-year-old close family friend [Minor] as the Minor had submitted a letter in support of the application (notwithstanding that the Applicants did not raise as a relevant factor the best interests of the Minor).

paragraphs.summary: Officer refused the second H&C application on January 23, 2020, considering Applicants' factors and best interests of a 16-year-old family friend who supported the application.

propositions.text: Officer's decision was unreasonable due to errors assessing establishment and hardship, and failure to conduct holistic assessment.
propositions.quote: The Applicants asserts that the Officer’s decision was unreasonable on the basis that the Officer erred in relation to their assessment of both the Applicants’ degree of establishment and the hardship that would arise if they returned to Brazil, and failed to conduct a holistic assessment of the Applicants’ H&C application.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue the Officer's decision was unreasonable due to errors assessing establishment, hardship, and failure to conduct holistic assessment.

propositions.text: Section 25(1) IRPA allows Minister discretion to grant permanent residence on humanitarian and compassionate grounds by weighing all relevant considerations cumulatively.
propositions.quote: Subsection 25(1) of the IRPA gives the Minister discretion to exempt foreign nationals from the ordinary requirements of that statute and grant permanent resident status in Canada if the Minister is of the opinion that such relief is justified by H&C considerations. An H&C determination under section 25(1) of the IRPA is a global one, where all the relevant considerations are to be weighed cumulatively in order to determine if relief is justified in the circumstances.

propositions.text: Relief is justified if circumstances would excite a reasonable person's desire to relieve another's misfortunes, per Kanthasamy and Caleb cases.
propositions.quote: Relief is considered justified if the circumstances would excite in a reasonable person in a civilized community a desire to relieve the misfortunes of another [see Kanthasamy v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 SCC 61 at paras 13, 28; Caleb v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 1018 at para 10].

paragraphs.summary: Section 25(1) IRPA allows Minister discretion to grant permanent residence on humanitarian and compassionate grounds by weighing all relevant considerations cumulatively; relief justified if reasonable person would desire to relieve misfortunes.

propositions.text: H&C exemptions are exceptional, highly discretionary, and deserve considerable court deference.
propositions.quote: The granting of an exemption for H&C reasons is deemed to be exceptional and highly discretionary and therefore “deserving of considerable deference by the Court” [see Qureshi v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 335 at para 30].

propositions.text: No rigid formula determines H&C outcomes, per Sivalingam case.
propositions.quote: There is no “rigid formula” that determines the outcome [see Sivalingam v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 1185 at para 7].

paragraphs.summary: H&C exemptions are exceptional, highly discretionary, deserving court deference; no rigid formula determines outcomes.

propositions.text: Standard of review for H&C decisions is reasonableness, requiring transparency, intelligibility, and justification.
propositions.quote: The applicable standard of review of an H&C decision is reasonableness [see Kanthasamy, supra at para 44]. In conducting a reasonableness review, a court must consider the outcome of the administrative decision in light of its underlying rationale, in order to ensure that the decision as a whole is transparent, intelligible and justified [see Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at para 15].

paragraphs.summary: Standard of review for H&C decisions is reasonableness, requiring transparency, intelligibility, and justification.

propositions.text: Officer's error on adverse country conditions in Brazil is significant enough to grant judicial review application.
propositions.quote: While the Applicants have raised a number of alleged errors made by the Officer in conducting their H&C analysis, I am satisfied that the error made by the Officer in relation to their assessment of the adverse country conditions in Brazil is sufficiently significant to warrant the granting of this application for judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: Officer's error on adverse country conditions in Brazil is significant enough to grant judicial review application.

propositions.text: Officer found Applicants likely negatively affected by poor economic conditions in Brazil, based on submitted reports and Applicants' inability to find employment.
propositions.quote: The applicants state that they would be negatively affected by adverse country conditions in Brazil, including poor economic conditions and gender discrimination in the work force. In support of these statements the applicants have submitted excerpts from several research reports concerning country conditions in Brazil. As well, the applicants’ H&C submissions state that the applicants were unable to obtain employment during the years that they resided in Brazil after returning from Canada. Accordingly, I find that the applicants’ H&C materials indicate that it is likely that the applicants would be negatively affected by poor economic conditions if the applicants were to return to Brazil.

propositions.text: Officer noted adverse country conditions are only one factor and H&C decision is based on all factors cumulatively.
propositions.quote: However, I note that this is only one of the factors for consideration on this H&C application and that an H&C decision is based on an assessment of all of the factors for consideration that are brought forward.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found Applicants likely negatively affected by poor economic conditions in Brazil but noted this is only one factor in H&C decision.

propositions.text: In H&C analysis, officer must assign weight to each factor and conduct a global cumulative assessment to determine if relief is justified.
propositions.quote: In conducting an H&C analysis, an officer must determine whether to assign a positive, negative or neutral weight to each factor raised by an applicant. Where a positive or negative weight is assigned, the officer must also determine the amount of weight to assign, often expressed as “significant”, “some” or “little” weight. The officer must then conduct a global assessment, where all of the relevant considerations are to be weighed cumulatively in order to determine if relief is justified in the circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: Officer must assign weight to each H&C factor and conduct a global cumulative assessment to decide if relief is justified.

propositions.text: Applicants requested adverse country conditions be weighed heavily in H&C application.
propositions.quote: In this case, the Applicants had requested that the adverse country conditions in Brazil be “weighed heavily”.

propositions.text: Officer found adverse country conditions likely negatively affect Applicants but gave no analysis or assigned weight to this factor.
propositions.quote: While the Officer found that “it is likely that the applicants would be negatively affected by poor economic conditions if the applicants were to return to Brazil”, the Officer conducted no analysis of how the adverse country conditions might impact the Applicants and thereafter made no corresponding determination of the weight to be assigned to this factor.

propositions.text: Officer's reasons are silent on weight assigned to adverse country conditions, preventing court from knowing if proper global assessment was done.
propositions.quote: In fact, a review of the entirety of the reasons reveals that they are silent as to the weight ultimately assigned to this factor by the Officer. This deficiency in the Officer’s reasons prevents the Court from knowing whether a proper global assessment was conducted.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants requested heavy weight for adverse country conditions; Officer found likely negative effect but gave no weight or analysis, preventing proper global assessment.

propositions.text: Officer's decision is not intelligible or justified; judicial review application allowed, decision set aside, matter remitted to different officer.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, I find that the Officer’s decision is neither intelligible nor adequately justified. As a result, the application for judicial review is allowed, the decision of the Officer is set aside and the matter is remitted to a different officer for redetermination.

paragraphs.summary: Officer's decision is not intelligible or justified; judicial review allowed, decision set aside, matter remitted to different officer.

propositions.text: No certified questions proposed or arise; judicial review allowed and matter remitted to another officer.
propositions.quote: The parties have proposed no certified questions and I agree that none arise. JUDGMENT in IMM-1654-20 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that: The application for judicial review is allowed and the matter is remitted to another officer for redetermination. The parties proposed no question for certification and none arises.

paragraphs.summary: No certified questions proposed or arise; judicial review allowed and matter remitted to another officer.
